analytic.title: Static Analysis of Run-Time Inter-Thread Interferences in Shared Cache Multi-Core Architectures based on Instruction Fetching Timing

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: For real-time systems, in order to provide the basis for schedulability analysis, it is crucial to obtain Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of applications, which is very challenging due to the possible runtime inter-thread interferences caused by shared resources in multi-core processors. For multi-core platforms with shared cache, instructions of a thread may be evicted by another co-running thread, which results in the interferences in shared cache. Designers need to consider the interferences while analyzing WCET of threads on multi-core platforms. This paper proposes a novel approach to analyzing the worst-case cache interferences based on instruction fetching timing, while judging the interferences status through instruction fetching timing relations. The paper presents an algorithm for instruction fetching timing based on Depth-First-Search in control flow graph. Our approach can reasonably estimate runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache by introducing timing relations analysis into address mapping method. Experiments show that our proposed approach improves the tightness of WCET estimation by 19.244% on average.

div.head: I.
div.p: INTRODUCTION With the scaling of technology and the diminishing return of complex mono-processors, multi-core chips have been increasingly adopted in microprocessor industry [1]. In particular, with the growing demand of high performance by high-end real-time applications, such as HDTV and video encoding/decoding standards, it is expected that multicore processors will be increasingly used in real-time systems for achieving higher performance/throughput cost-effectively. Even if multicore processors may offer potential benefits to embedded systems, so far it is hardly widely used in embedded systems, even impossible. For real-time systems, especially hard real-time systems, it is crucial to obtain the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of each real-time task, which will provide the basis for schedulability analysis and performance checking. However, multi-core computing platforms further aggravate the complexity of WCET analysis due to the possible runtime inter-thread interferences in shared resources, especially shared hardware resources, such as shared cache or bus, which are very difficult to analyze statically. In multi-core processors, shared resources may be accessed by co-running multi-tasks at the same time, and when a task accesses shared resources it may be interfered by other tasks, which results that its execution time is changed and WCET analysis becomes more difficult. In multi-core architectures, the validation and safeness of WCET analysis is correlational to modeling and analysis of shared resources.

Shared Cache has been increasingly adopted by multicore architectures to improve performance of multi-core processors as well as utilization of Cache [2] [3]. But the memory structure of shared cache will result in interferences among threads [4] [5], that is to say, a task running on a core may evict some data in shared cache, which is needed by tasks running on another core. Therefore the execution time of tasks cannot be computed separately and interferences caused by shared cache among co-running threads must be considered. However, researchers in the WCET analysis community agree that "it will be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to develop analysis methods that can accurately capture the contention among multiple cores in a shared cache" [6].

Some works already deal with the problem of analyzability in the presence of shared resources. In multicore architecture, some tasks may have heavy accesses to shared cache. Anderson et al. [7] [8] discourage the coscheduling of such threads (or tasks), shared cache contention can be reduced dramatically. Although improved cache performance can straightforward reduce average execution costs, it is still unknown how to obtain the WCET of each real-time thread in their system model because interferences cannot be completely avoided. Researches [9][10] presented a scheduling strategy for real-time tasks with both timing and cache space constraints, which allows each task to use a fixed number of cache partitions. The purpose of such techniques is to completely avoid conflicts on shared resources to ensure predictable timing behaviors. Then the WCET analysis techniques of mono-core can be adopted by multi-core architectures. Although such techniques design a predictable cache structure, such structure will result in low usage of cache and high performance of co-running threads in multi-core processors cannot be obtained. Yan et al. [11] statically analyzed the worst-case instruction access interferences between different threads based on program control flow information. While Yan et al.'s work can achieve tighter WCET estimation than a conservative approach by assuming all L2 accesses are misses, there is still large structural overestimation and timing order overestimation as compared to the observed WCET results.

All these researches analyzed shared cache multi-core architectures through programs' logic structure and cache structure. They all based on a simple common assumption: whatever kind of execution, instructions from two threads mapping to the same cache line must be interfered with each other. However, in actual run-time, interferences do not always occur because of some other factors, for example, execution order and execution timing. So abovementioned assumption is too conservative to obtain tight WCET estimation.

To our best knowledge, most recent researches do not take instruction fetching timing into consideration. In this paper we first introduce consideration on instruction fetching timing based on address mapping. Through analyzing fetching timing relations among instructions we can estimate ___________________________________ 978-1-4244-8728-8/11/$26.00 ©2011 IEEE runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache more reasonably, which can improve the tightness of WCET estimation. In this paper we make the following contributions:

x Our approach first introduces timing factor into address mapping factor on the analysis of interthread interferences in shared cache, which can estimate the maximum inter-thread cache interferences more reasonably.

x For the problem that Zhang-Yan [12] considered, our approach can obtain inter-thread cache interferences value, 0, from Zhang-Yan's 1. Compared with Zhang-Yan's approach, our result is more close to the actual run-time execution. For the inter-thread cache interferences where there is no logic access problem, we can estimate inter-thread cache interferences more reasonably and tighter.

x Finally, we can tighter the WCET estimation of multi-core architectures than previous approaches. To sum up, we propose a finer-grain approach based on instruction fetching timing and consider timing relations among instructions to obtain inter-thread interferences, which is much close to the actual execution. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed approach can improve the tightness of WCET estimation by 13.7% on average, as compared to Yan et al.'s approach.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. First, we describe the instruction fetching timing influence on the inter-thread cache interferences on multi-core architectures, which is also the research background of this paper. Then we introduce the proposed approach based on instruction fetching timing to analyze the worst-case inter-thread interferences in shared cache in Section II. In Section III, we detail the idea to obtain instruction fetching timing. Section IV gives the experimental results. Finally, we draw conclusions and future work in Section V.

div.head: II. STATIC ANALYSIS OF RUNTIME INTER-THREAD INTERFERENCES IN SHARED CACHE MULTI-CORE ARCHITECTURES BASED ON INSTRUCTION FETCHING TIMING
div.p: In shared cache multi-core architectures, threads will be interfered by co-running threads while accessing shared cache. Therefore, we need to take runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache into consideration on analyzing threads WCET. First, we analyze relations between runtime inter-thread interferences and instruction fetching timing. Then we present a WCET analysis method based instruction fetching timing, by which we can judge runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache through the timing relations among instructions.

div.head: A. Relations between Instruction Fetching Timing Relations and Runtime Inter-thread Interferences
div.p: Runtime inter-thread interferences in shared instruction cache are much related to instruction fetching timing. For example, in a dual-core processor, we assume that two threads, Thread a and Thread b , are running in a dual-core processor consisting of Core0 and Core1. Core0 is running Thread a and Core1is running Thread b , as depicted in Figure 2. It is assumed that instruction ai and aj from Thread a are mapped to the same cache line to instruction bm from Thread b . Instruction ai is the first one in the cache line. A cold miss occurs when ai tries to access cache and instructions of the whole cache block are fetched into the cache line. So a cache hit occurs when aj accesses cache. However, the access of instruction ai may be interfered by the co-running thread Thread b , if the instruction fetching timing of bm is (1) after that of ai and before that of aj: the cache line content will be replaced by instruction bm when bm accesses cache. So when aj accesses cache a cache miss occurs instead of a cache hit, aj is interfered by bm, as case2 in Table I. (2) Before that of ai or after that of aj: the execution of instruction bm will not interfere with ai and aj, as the case1 and case2 in Table I. , then inter-thread interferences will not occur.

div.head: B. Static Analysis of Runtime Inter-Thread Interferences in Shared Cache based on Instruction Fetching Timing
div.p: In shared cache multi-core architectures, threads may be interfered by co-running threads while accessing shared cache. Therefore, we need to take runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache into consideration on analyzing threads WCET.

If a private L1 cache miss occurs during threads execution, then processor cores will access shared cache when runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache may happen. Based on the L1 cache miss, we begin to analyze shared cache access. When the access to shared cache(for example shared L2 cache) is cache miss caused by thread itself, viz. cold miss, the instruction in shared cache is L2 miss and we do not need to analyze runtime inter-thread interferences. When the access to shared cache is cache hit, we need to check whether the cache hit is changed by corunning threads or not, that is to say, we need to analyze runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache. First the interfering instructions set is found, then our approach needs to analyze the instruction fetching timing to determine runtime inter-thread interferences: (1) If all instructions of the interfering set satisfy the instructions fetching timing relations of non-interference, the current instruction will not be interfered and the access is L2 hit; (2) Otherwise the current instruction will be interfered and the access is changed from L2 hit to L2 miss. Algorithm 1 gives the details.

div.head: A. Basic Idea
div.p: In order to compute the execution timing in basic block, researches [13] [14] first proposed execution graph to model dependences and resource contentions and use iterative method to obtain the execution timing in basic block. While we aim to obtain the instruction fetching timing through whole program instead of in basic block, so we apply the idea of execution graph to obtain the timing through whole program. We start from the first basic block and use DFS algorithm to analyze the instruction fetching timing of next basic block based on the known execution timing of current basic block.

For the first basic block B 0 , the first instruction of B 0 starts execution at time 0, so we can use the idea in [13] [14] to obtain its instruction fetching timing. However, for other basic blocks, B i , because its first instruction does not start at time 0, instruction fetching timing cannot be obtained only by the idea. We need to consider the timing of blocks preceding B i and influence of basic blocks succeeding B i . The instruction fetching timing of B i is not a simple addition of basic blocks preceding B i . That is because that there are pipeline constraints, resource contentions and data dependences. In summary, we construct execution graph based on prologue and epilogue to analyze the instruction fetching timing of B i through whole program.

x time intervals for prologue: In execution graph, each node v is represented by the instruction identifier and pipeline stages, for the typical five stage pipeline a node can be IF(I k ), ID(I k ), EX(I k ), WB(I k ) and CM(I k ). There are some parameters to describe the execution information of each node: ready, start and finish. Research [13] [14] . For the instruction fetching timing through whole program, we cannot assume that the first instruction start at time 0. We need to consider execution timing of prologue.

During the DFS, the instruction fetching timing of instructions along current path is known, viz. we have obtain the execution timing of B i 's prologue. There are three kinds of relations between instructions in prologue and B i :

(1) Pipeline constraints as in full I-buffer and ROB: Assuming I-buffer has FQ_len entries, there will be no entry available for IF(I (i+FQ_len) ) before the completion of ID(I i ).Therefore there should be a dependence between them. Similarly, with ROB_len-entry ROB, there should be a dependence between CM(I i ) and ID(I (i+ROB_len) ). We can determine the ready time of IF and ID nodes by these two constraints.

(2) Data dependences among instructions: If an instruction in prologue produces a result that is used by an instruction in current basic block, then prologue should make effects on body, viz. data dependence. We can determine the ready time of EX nodes by data dependencies, which will make effects on the time of IF.

(3) Resource contentions: If an instruction in prologue contends for a functional unit with instructions in B i , then the execution of prologue will affect B i . We can determine the start time of EX nodes in B i .

Figure 2 shows the execution graph constructed from B i and prologue. With the constraints of ROB, there are ROB_len instructions in pipeline at most, for example, I i , I (i+1) , I (i+2) ,…, I (i+ROB_len-1) , then the last (ROB_len-1) instructions may have late contentions with I i . Consequently the time of EX(I i ) node will be affected by these instructions. For current basic block, B i , the last (ROB_len-1) instructions may be contended by epilogue: I (+1) , I (+2) , … , I (ROB_len-1) .

Instruction fetching timing of B i through whole program can be obtained by the known execution timing information of prologue. After that the execution timing information of epilogue also will be obtained based on the known B i . Then we can analyze the late contentions between epilogue and current basic block B i . The late contentions have effects on EX nodes of B i , and the effects will be passed to CM nodes through pipeline. With the constraints as in full I-buffer and ROB, at last the effects are passed to IF nodes. In summary, the late contentions caused by epilogue affects execution timing of IF nodes, viz. instruction fetching timing. We can see that for B i , only EX and CM nodes will be affected, not IF nodes. That is to say instruction fetching timing of B i will be not affected. However, when DFS goes from B i to next basic block, B i+1 , the changes of EX and CM will affect instruction fetching timing of B i+1 . So we need to analyze the late contentions of epilogue to B i .

div.head: B. Algorithm
div.p: We present an algorithm called IF_Time_in_Program to estimate instruction fetching timing of Bi through the whole program based on known prologue and considering epilogue's effects, as algorithm 2 shows. First, according to abovementioned pipeline constraints and dependencies, some nodes of Bi are affected by prologue. We can obtain execution timing information of these nodes based on the known prologue. Then the process of the nodes proceed in topologically sorted order and start from IF nodes of the first instruction to compute execution timing of other nodes. Meanwhile we analyze the effects of epilogue on current basic block. At last the algorithm invokes EarliestTime and LatestTime to iteratively analyze instruction fetching timing. IV. EVALUATION METHODOLOGY In the microarchitecture analysis, we introduce the modeling and analysis of runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache to estimate multi-core WCET. The experimental results are compared with the simulated performance to evaluate the validation and tightness of our approach.

div.head: A. Experimental Framework
div.p: The WCET analysis for multi-core processors is based on extending Chronos [15] timing analysis tool. Chronos is originally a single core WCET analysis tool. We have extended it to implement the proposed runtime inter-thread interferences analysis and WCET estimation for multi-core processors by introducing shared cache analysis.

To compare the worst-case performance with the average-case performance (i.e., the simulated performance based on typical inputs), we use SESC simulator [16] to simulate a dual-core processor, in which each core is a 2issue superscalar processor with 5 pipeline stages. The important parameters of the dual-core memory hierarchy are given in Table II. The benchmarks are selected from SNU [17] real-time benchmarks.

div.head: B. Schemes Studied
div.p: We classify interfering factors in shared cache as: (1) Addressing of Interference: two instructions are considered to interfere with each other if both are mapped to same cache line. (2)Timing of Interference: Based on factor (1), instruction fetching timing is taken into consideration to analyze runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache.

In order to evaluate the factor (2), Timing of Interference, we chose matmul as the co-running thread, whose big code size can discourage the factor (1), Addressing of Interference. We do some modification to matmul:
(1) First, in order to give a simple and intuitionistic test, we unroll matmul to eliminate loops, named as matmulunrolling.

(2) Second, in order to evaluate factor (2), we triple the number of loops, named as matmul-3, which broaden the instruction fetching timing frame and the possibility of interthread interferences increases.

div.head: C. Experimental results
div.p: Table III compares the WCET-m-u (Addressing of Interference), which only considers address mapping with the WCET estimated by our approach, WCET-m-u (Timing of Interference), which considers instruction fetching timing. For L1 miss, the cache miss of access to shared cache has two statuses: (1) cold: cold misses caused by thread itself and (2) interf: misses caused by co-running threads. As we can see, for WCET-m-u (Addressing of Interference), besides cold misses, all other accesses to shared cache are misses because of co-running thread. While for WCET-m-u (Timing of Interference), not all the accesses to shared cache are misses. For example, for bs, there are 5 misses caused by the interferences of matmul-unrolling when only considering address mapping while only 3 misses when considering instruction fetching timing. Average 63.534% of inter-thread interferences are not misses because of instruction fetching timing. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed approach can improve the tightness of WCET estimation by 12.702% on average, as compared to the method which only considers address mapping.

In order to evaluate the validation and tightness of our proposed approach, we compare the observed results, results only considering address mapping and considering instruction fetching timing, as shown in Table IV. As can be seen in the last column of Table IV, the estimated WCET obtained by our approach is not too far from the observed WCET for most benchmarks. However, for the method only considering address mapping, it is farther than our approach, which is because our approach takes instruction fetching timing into consideration on runtime inter-thread interferences in shared cache and can reasonably estimate the upper bound of WCET. The proposed approach can improve the tightness of WCET estimation by 19.244% on average.

Although our approach can achieve a tight bound for most of the benchmarks, we notice that there are still overestimations for some applications. The overestimation in our WCET analysis mainly comes from two sources. (1) Loop structure affects instruction fetching timing and it need to consider the iteration times and execution time of loops, which is difficult to be determined. (2) Branch structure also makes effects.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: This paper proposes a novel approach to analyzing the inter-thread interferences in shared cache. We take instruction fetching timing into consideration based on address mapping and analyze inter-thread interferences through the sufficient and unnecessary condition of noninterference, which improve the tightness of threads WCET in multi-core architectures. Our experiments indicate that the proposed approach improves the tightness of WCET estimation by 19.244% on average.

Loop and branch structures make effects on instruction fetching timing and in future work we plan to further enhance the tightness of the static analysis for shared caches through accurately analyzing threads structures.
